prompt.context: The year is 1999, in the middle of the .Com-boom. An airline was approached by a group of entrepreneurs. The entrepreneurs offered the airline to invest $100MM in their software company for 20% equity, and also be the first customer for the software they develop. The software is an e-marketplace where airliners and spare parts suppliers could meet to improve the purchasing capabilities of the airlines and to reduce the purchasing costs. Aircraft parts are obviously a hugely important part of the airline business, as airlines struggle to keep planes in the air as much as possible, minimize downtime and control costs.
prompt.question: What should the airline do?

clarifying_info.q: How does the airline currently purchase spare parts?
clarifying_info.a: The airline currently has a legacy system. The system is not that suitable to what is actually happening and therefore there is a lot of extra phone calls and process work happening.

clarifying_info.q: How much does a purchasing transaction cost an airline?
How many transactions does each airline perform every year?
clarifying_info.a: 500,000 for each of the airlines in the US

clarifying_info.q: How many airlines are there in the US?
How much will a transaction cost in the new system?
clarifying_info.a: $6 payment for the software company and $9 internal costs (labor, systems, etc.) — total $15 per transaction

clarifying_info.q: Is there any other cost a customer needs to pay to join?
What is the cost structure for the software company?
clarifying_info.a: No variable costs. $10MM a year to pay for corporate expenses.

clarifying_info.q: Will the E-Market allow increased bargaining power?
clarifying_info.a: The aircraft industry and the spare parts industry specifically are highly regulated. To become an approved FAA supplier costs money and therefore barriers to entry are significant. Each part has one or two suppliers at most, so bargaining power will not improve with the E-Market.

exhibits.title: E-Market Structure
exhibits.shows: A diagram showing the E-Market platform connecting Airline 1 through Airline 20 on one side and Supplier 1 through Supplier 1000 on the other side
exhibits.data: 20 airlines connected to E-Market; 1000 suppliers connected to E-Market

framework: Decouple the two distinct decisions: (1) investment decision — should the airline invest $100MM for 20% equity, and (2) customer decision — should the airline join as a customer (first or later)
Investment analysis: assess expected cash flows, implied valuation, and required return on the $100MM outlay
Customer analysis: quantify cost savings vs. licensing fee, assess payback period, and weigh first-customer risks
Market context: size of addressable market, competitive dynamics, network effects (supplier and airline adoption), and regulatory environment
Strategic fit: alignment with core operations, capital availability, and long-term role in the e-marketplace ecosystem

questions.prompt: Calculate the expected annual cash flow from the $100MM investment (20% equity stake in the software company).
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute total platform revenues, subtract fixed costs to get net income, then apply the 20% ownership share. Should then convert to NPV or payback logic and conclude whether the return justifies the investment.

math.setup: Annual revenue = transaction fee × transactions per airline × number of airlines; Profit = revenue – fixed costs; Airline share = profit × 20%
steps: NPV check: at 20% discount rate for software industry, perpetuity value = $10MM / 20% = $50MM, vs. $100MM invested → value destruction from day 1
math.answer: Annual return of $10MM on a $100MM investment implies a 10-year undiscounted payback. At a 20% software-industry discount rate the perpetuity value is only $50MM — the investment destroys half its value immediately. This is a bad investment.

questions.prompt: Calculate the net benefit of joining the E-Market as a customer.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute per-transaction savings, annualise, then compare to licensing fee for payback. Should then identify first-customer-specific risks that reduce the expected return.

math.setup: Savings per transaction = current cost – new cost; Annual savings = savings per transaction × transactions; Payback = licensing fee / annual savings
math.answer: As a customer the airline recoups its $20MM licensing fee in roughly 1.1 years — an attractive proposition. However, being the FIRST customer carries meaningful incremental risk.

questions.prompt: What are the specific risks of being the FIRST customer vs. a later adopter?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates distinguish first-customer risk from steady-state customer value: supplier adoption may be low initially (limiting efficiency gains), software may have bugs early on, and the software company could fail — losing the $20MM licensing fee with no returns.

questions.prompt: (Challenge question) The E-Market introduces a feature that lets airlines view each other's spare-parts inventory by location. Is this a good feature?
questions.guidance: Full answer covers: (1) industry benefit — reduces downtime and costs across all airlines; (2) moral-hazard risk — airlines may reduce their own inventory if they can always borrow from peers; (3) mitigation — implement a parts-exchange account per airline, credited when a part is provided and debited when a part is borrowed, capped at a minimum balance (e.g. –$5MM), creating a balanced incentive structure that encourages participation while maintaining adequate industry-wide inventory.

brainstorming.prompt: What risks and considerations should the airline weigh as the first customer of the E-Market?

categories.name: Supplier adoption risk
ideas: Not all suppliers will join immediately or at all
Low supplier participation limits the efficiency and cost-savings promised by the platform
FAA certification barriers mean supplier universe is already limited

categories.name: Technology/execution risk
ideas: Software will have bugs in the first months or years as a new product
Integration with the airline's legacy systems may be complex and costly
Downtime or errors in the platform could disrupt critical spare-parts procurement

categories.name: Financial/counterparty risk
ideas: Software company could go bankrupt, making the $20MM licensing fee unrecoverable
20% equity stake loses value if company fails
No variable costs for the platform means fixed-cost leverage cuts both ways

categories.name: Strategic/competitive risk
ideas: First-mover disadvantage: absorbing teething problems competitors avoid
Competitors who join later get a proven, lower-risk product at the same price
Sharing inventory data (in the advanced feature) could expose strategic information

recommendation: Do NOT invest $100MM for 20% equity: the undiscounted payback is 10 years and the NPV at a software-industry discount rate of 20% is only $50MM — half the investment is destroyed immediately.

Do join as a customer — but NOT as the first customer unless compensated for first-mover risks: payback as a customer is ~1.1 years, which is excellent, but early-adopter risks (bugs, low supplier penetration, vendor bankruptcy) meaningfully reduce expected returns.
Consider joining after two or three other airlines have adopted the platform, validating supplier coverage and software stability.
risks: Supplier ecosystem may never reach critical mass given FAA certification barriers
Software company may fail before the airline recoups its licensing fee
Being first customer may mean bearing integration and debugging costs that later customers avoid
Inventory-sharing feature (if introduced) could create moral hazard and reduce individual airline inventory discipline
next_steps: Negotiate a first-customer discount or risk-sharing arrangement (e.g. milestone-based licensing fee) if asked to join early
Monitor supplier sign-up rate before committing the licensing fee
Reassess the investment decision if the platform grows and the equity stake becomes purchasable at a more favourable valuation
